read.sections.0.text.note: FAITH VOCABULARY. 'Tín đồ Hồi giáo, Kitô giáo và Do Thái giáo' for 'Muslims, Christians and Jews'; 'Thượng đế' for 'God' (a Muslim reviewer may prefer 'Allah' or 'Thượng đế', a Jewish reviewer may have a different preference). 'Tín đồ Ấn Độ giáo' for Hindus, and the cycle of creation-end-creation: a Hindu reviewer should check it. 'Các bậc tổ tiên' for 'ancestral beings' and 'Thổ dân ở Úc' for Aboriginal peoples of Australia: an Aboriginal-aware reviewer should check these terms and that 'tổ tiên' does not sound like ordinary human ancestors. | Review: English says animals; 'muôn loài' is broader. Also 'bậc tổ tiên' for 'ancestral beings' may read as human ancestors; native/Aboriginal-informed reviewer should check. FAITH string: Hồi giáo/Kitô giáo/Do Thái giáo/Ấn Độ giáo, Thượng đế, Thổ dân Úc. [Reviewer changed: muôn loài → muôn thú]
read.sections.0.text.source: People all over the world have asked where the world came from. Many communities have an origin account. It tells how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as a great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is made, ends and then begins again. Many Aboriginal peoples of Australia tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, the water and the animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass on their own accounts in stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, like the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Accounts like these carry a group's beliefs and values.
read.sections.0.text.back: People all over the world have asked where this world comes from. Many communities have an origin account. That account says how something began. Many Muslim, Christian and Jewish believers believe that God created heaven and earth. Many Hindu believers see time as one great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is created, ends, then begins again from the start. Many Aboriginal groups in Australia tell of ancestors who made the land, water and all living things. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass down their own accounts through stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, like the founding story of the village at Tallgrass Valley. Such accounts carry the beliefs and values of a group of people.

'Các vị ấy' for the ancestral beings: check the respectful pronoun. | Review: FAITH string. 'Thượng đế' for God across Muslim/Christian/Jewish believers; check with a member of each faith (Muslim reviewers may prefer 'Allah' / 'Thượng đế'). 'bậc tổ tiên' for ancestral beings.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: People all over the world ask how it all began. Many groups have an origin account. It tells how things began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God made the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and starts again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of beings from long ago. These beings made the land and the animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific have their own accounts. Our made-up town, Tallgrass Valley, has one too. These accounts hold beliefs and values.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: People everywhere ask where things began. Many groups have an origin account. That account says how things began. Many Muslim, Christian and Jewish believers believe that God made the world. Many Hindu believers believe that the world ends and then begins again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal groups tell of ancestors from ancient times. Those beings made the land and the animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific also have their own accounts. Our imaginary town of Tallgrass Valley also has an account. These accounts keep beliefs and values.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Each account answers a different kind of question

read.sections.1.text.note: 'Lời kể' is used for faith AND science accounts, as 'account' is in English. 'Một lời kể khoa học' might sound odd (science explains rather than 'tells'); alternative 'cách giải thích khoa học'. 'Đức tin' for 'faith' (KEY_TERMS suggests 'niềm tin' for belief). 'Không ngừng mở rộng' for 'has been growing' (universe expanding); a science teacher may prefer 'giãn nở'. 13,8 tỉ năm: confirm 'tỉ' (not 'tỷ') for the school style. | Review: FAITH string: 'lời kể theo đức tin' vs science; not ranked, but 'lời kể' (account/telling) for faith may sound like 'story' to a believer. Native reviewer should decide whether 'lời kể' is respectful enough.
read.sections.1.text.source: Each kind of account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been growing ever since. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer other questions. Why is there a world? What matters most? How should people treat each other? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an account, when, and why. Look again at the three questions about beginnings. Each one needs a different kind of answer.
read.sections.1.text.back: Each kind of account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things in nature happen. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and since then has kept expanding without stopping. Faith accounts and a culture's accounts often answer other questions. Why is there this world? What matters most? How should people treat one another? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an account, when, and why. Look again at the three questions about the beginning. Each needs a different kind of answer.

read.sections.2.heading.source: We learn about accounts with respect
read.sections.2.heading.back: We learn about accounts with respect

read.sections.2.text.note: Core of the respectful stance: 'chế giễu' (mock), 'phán xét hay xếp hạng' (judge or rank), 'Nhiều người tin rằng ...' and 'Các nhà khoa học giải thích rằng ...'. Reviewers: confirm these model phrases are natural and neutral. 'Người có đức tin' for 'people of faith'. | Review: FAITH string: respect rules; checked, no ranking.
read.sections.2.text.source: In this lesson, we learn about accounts, but we do not judge them or rank them. Respect means describing each account carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe ..." for a faith account and "Scientists explain ..." for a science account. Many people hold both a faith account and a science account, and many scientists are also people of faith. Nobody has to share what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an account, check a trusted source or ask a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.back: In this lesson, we learn about accounts, but we do not judge or rank them. Respect means describing each account carefully and never mocking it. For a faith account, we say "Many people believe that ...". For a scientific account, we say "Scientists explain that ...". Many people hold both a faith account and a scientific account, and many scientists are also people of faith. No one has to say what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an account, look at a trustworthy source or ask your teacher.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: 'Cười nhạo' for mock; 'chấp nhận cả hai loại lời kể' for 'accept both kinds of account'. Check 'chấp nhận' does not sound like 'put up with'; 'cùng tin cả hai' may be better.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Here, we learn about accounts. We do not judge them. We do not say one is best. Respect means we describe each account with care. We never laugh at it. Say "Many people believe" for faith. Say "Scientists explain" for science. Many people accept both kinds of account. You do not have to share your own beliefs.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Here, we learn about accounts. We do not judge them. We do not say which account is best. Respect means describing each account carefully. We never laugh at any account. For faith, say "Many people believe that". For science, say "Scientists explain that". Many people accept both kinds of accounts. You do not have to say what you believe.

write.example.source: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people could use evidence that scientists measure. For example, they study light from faraway stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer it, people could listen to the elders. They could think about the promise to share the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One asks how something happened in nature. The other asks what matters to a group of people.
write.example.back: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people can use evidence that scientists measure. For example, they study light from distant stars. They can also think about the promise to share the fruit of the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One is about how something happens in nature. The other asks about what matters to a group of people.

watch.summary.source: This video gives a science account of how the universe began. Scientists explain that it began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first, it was very small and very hot. Since then, it has grown bigger and cooler. Scientists use evidence they can measure. For example, they see that faraway groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still growing. They also find a faint glow left over from when the universe was very young. A science account like this answers questions about how things happen in nature. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need other kinds of answers. Many people value both a science account and a faith account.
watch.summary.back: This video gives a scientific account of how the universe began. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first it was very small and very hot. Since then it has grown and cooled. Scientists use evidence that they can measure. For example, they see that groups of stars very far away are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still expanding. They also found a faint glow left over from when the universe was very young. A scientific account like this answers questions about how things happen in nature. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need other kinds of answers. Many people value both scientific accounts and faith accounts.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Please ask a local educator, ideally from the learners' own communities, to review this lesson before it is used. Most pilot learners are likely to come from Muslim-majority communities, and others hold different beliefs or none.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Ask a local educator, ideally someone from the learners' own community, to look over this lesson before using it. Many learners in the pilot may come from mostly Muslim communities, and others have different beliefs or no religion.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Never ask learners to state, defend or rank their own beliefs. If a learner shares a belief, thank them and move on; do not debate it.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Never ask a learner to state, defend or rank their own beliefs. If a learner shares their beliefs, thank them and move on; do not argue about it.

sensitiveNotes.2.source: The lesson describes faith accounts only in general terms and does not retell any scripture. If you add an example, keep it general and check the wording with someone from that tradition.
